intro: Boston lost its two most famous trees long ago: the Liberty Tree to a Loyalist axe in 1775 and the Great Elm of the Common to a storm in 1876. What survived is stranger. Two English elms have flanked the Shaw Memorial since around 1800, and the Arnold Arboretum keeps accession cards on its trees like a library catalogue. Below: a Common and Public Garden pair, seven in the Arboretum including a bonsai begun in 1737, three in Cambridge, and in Danvers a pear planted in the 1630s that still fruits beside a hospital car park. All are free.
meta_description: Boston's remarkable trees, from the elms flanking the Shaw Memorial to a tree extinct in the wild at the Arnold Arboretum. Locations, stories, sources.
question_meta: Boston's oldest documented trees are the Shaw Memorial elms on the Common, planted between 1772 and 1812. Their story, and what else to see.
question_answer: The oldest documented landscape trees in Boston are the two English Elms flanking the Shaw Memorial on Boston Common, planted between 1772 and 1812. Older still and small enough for a table is the Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress at the Arnold Arboretum, a bonsai begun in 1737. The oldest tree on this list stands outside the city: the Endicott Pear in Danvers, about 25 km north, planted in the 1630s.
question_context: Boston's relationship with its trees is a long ledger of documented losses, and that is precisely what makes the survivors verifiable. The Liberty Tree, the elm under which the Sons of Liberty gathered, was felled by Loyalists in August 1775 and the city has marked the spot ever since. The Great Elm of the Common, once called the city's oldest inhabitant, blew down in 1876 and was mourned in print. The Public Garden's lagoon willow, the most photographed tree in the city, collapsed as recently as July 2026. Each loss was recorded, which means each survivor stands in an unusually well-documented landscape. Seven of them stand in the Arnold Arboretum, which keeps an accession-level GIS with a coordinate, a condition and a last-inspection date for every plant it holds. That is better than any tree register on this site, and it moved two pins here: the Franklin tree by 315 metres and the Wilson paperbark maple by 255, both to the exact accession our own sources already named. Where it offers two candidates and nothing separates them, as with the white oak on Peters Hill, the pin stays approximate rather than guessing.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Boston?
faq.a: The two English Elms flanking the Shaw Memorial on Boston Common, planted between 1772 and 1812, are the oldest documented trees growing in Boston ground. Older still is the Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress at the Arnold Arboretum, a bonsai begun in Japan in 1737. Outside the city, the Endicott Pear in Danvers was planted in the 1630s and is the oldest tree on this list.

faq.q: Is the Liberty Tree still standing?
faq.a: No. The Liberty Tree, the elm where Boston's revolutionary protests gathered, was felled by Loyalists in August 1775. A plaque and a bas-relief mark the site at Washington and Essex Streets; no tree on this list claims its mantle.

faq.q: Are Boston's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: All thirteen are free. Two stand on Boston Common and in the Public Garden, seven in the Arnold Arboretum (open free daily, Orange Line to Forest Hills), three across the river in Cambridge, and one, the Endicott Pear, in Danvers, where it is seen through its fence beside a hospital car park.

faq.q: What is a Franklinia and why does Boston have one?
faq.a: Franklinia alatamaha is a small flowering tree that has been extinct in the wild since the early 1800s; every living one descends from seeds collected in Georgia before then. The Arnold Arboretum's specimen, accessioned in 1905, flowers in late summer.

trees.name: The Shaw Memorial Elms
trees.age_estimate: planted between 1772 and 1812, so roughly 214 to 254 years old

location.address: Boston Common, opposite 24 Beacon Street (flanking the Robert Gould Shaw Memorial, corner of Beacon and Park Streets)

trees.story: Augustus Saint-Gaudens's memorial to Robert Gould Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th was built around these two elms, not the other way round. The trees came first, planted somewhere between 1772 and 1812, probably under the 1780 permission to plant elms across from John Hancock's mansion while he was governor. The bronze arrived in 1897 and sits on a vault designed to spare their roots. The Boston Globe calls them the oldest English elms in the Western Hemisphere. One caveat on the species. Two institutional sources and the memorial's own conservation record call them English elm; a single minority account describes them as American elm. The weight of evidence sits with English elm, but the disagreement is real. Their survival is not luck. In 1927 they were written off as close to dead. The arborist Henry Davis began treating them free of charge in the 1970s and the care has never stopped: bricks packed inside the hollow trunks for stability, six to eight feet taken off the crowns in 2013, inspections every fortnight. That retrenchment pruning is what gives them the blunt, cut back outline they carry through winter. Even the cramped root vault helps, densifying the wood against Dutch elm disease. Prunings have been turned into pens and sold. The two of them stand where the Freedom Trail meets Beacon and Park, shading the regiment they now outlive by more than a century.

trees.name: The Peters Hill White Oak
trees.age_estimate: roughly 195 to 220 years, core-sampled in 2018 to a germination date in the early 1800s

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, northeast slope of Peters Hill, above the crabapple (Malus) collection
location.neighbourhood: Peters Hill, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: Harvard's Arnold Arboretum has been cataloguing plants since 1872 and did not get round to this one until 2010. It shows up on an 1894 city survey of Peters Hill, already growing wild on ground the Arboretum later absorbed, so when it was finally accessioned it went into the books as found growing in place rather than planted. It may be the oldest tree in the entire landscape. In 2018 a core taken from the southwest stem gave 142 countable rings, with perhaps 60 more lost in a hollow centre, putting germination in the early 1800s. It is double leadered, two stems fused near the base with the seam still visible, roughly 17 metres tall and spreading 28 metres over the crabapple collection below it. A 1927 bird's eye map of the Arboretum drew it as a lone shepherd guarding an endless flock, the flock at the time being hawthorns that have since been replaced. Two honest notes. Everything known about this tree comes from the Arboretum itself, rigorous work with published ring counts, but we found nothing independent of the institution. And no coordinates are published, so the pin is the northeast slope of Peters Hill above the crabapples rather than the trunk. Walk up the slope and look for the widest crown on the hill. At that spread it is not a difficult hunt.

trees.name: The Franklin Tree of the Explorers Garden
trees.age_estimate: roughly 121 years (accessioned as a rooted cutting in 1905)

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, Explorers Garden (grid EG-8), Bussey Hill
location.neighbourhood: Bussey Hill, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: There is no wild Franklinia anywhere on earth and there has not been for about two hundred years. John Bartram found the species growing on a few acres beside the Altamaha River in Georgia in 1765, his son William collected seed around 1776, and within roughly fifty years the wild population was gone and never seen again. Every Franklin tree alive today, in every garden in the world, descends from that one collection. This is one of the oldest of them. The Arnold Arboretum took it in as a rooted cutting in 1905 from a Pennsylvania nursery, on a line traceable back to material from 1884. The International Dendrology Society, which has no stake in Harvard's reputation, calls it the largest and oldest known example of the species anywhere, and photographed it standing in October 2025. It is a small tree in the tea family and the only member of its genus, and it flowers on an odd schedule. Large cream white flowers with a boss of yellow stamens open late in the season, so the last of them are still out while the leaves around them are turning red. Seeing both at once on the same branch is the reason to come. It grows in the Explorers Garden on Bussey Hill. No coordinates are published for the individual plant, so the pin is the garden and the labels there take you the rest of the way.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood of the Public Garden

location.address: Boston Public Garden, near the Charles Street / Beacon Street corner of the Lagoon

trees.story: Until 1944 this species was known only from fossils and assumed to have been extinct for millions of years. Then living Metasequoia turned up in Sichuan, and in early 1948 the first seeds to leave China arrived at Harvard's Arnold Arboretum in Jamaica Plain, a few miles from where this tree stands, just ahead of the door closing on scientific exchange with China for decades. The Arboretum raised seedlings and sent them around the world. This one was planted in the Public Garden in 1963, one of four here. It is not old, and it is not pretending to be. At about 63 it earns its place on what it is rather than how long it has stood. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer, which most people meet for the first time in autumn, when a tree that plainly looks like a redwood turns foxy orange and drops every needle it has. The trunk is fluted and deeply hollowed under each branch, another oddity of the species, and a younger 'Gold Rush' cultivar stands across the path for comparison. One note on sourcing: the 1963 planting date and the exact placement come from the Friends of the Public Garden, whose own people care for the tree, and we found no record of this specimen independent of them.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn foxy orange and fall

trees.name: The Original Dawn Redwood of the Arboretum
trees.age_estimate: roughly 77 years, grown from seed collected in Hubei, China in 1948

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, near the Hunnewell Visitor Center, opposite the Arborway Gate

trees.story:
This tree grew from the seed shipment that put a fossil back into the ground. In 1948 the Arnold Arboretum took delivery of seed collected in Hubei, China, from a species that had been known to science only from fossils until living trees turned up in the interior a few years earlier. The seed was raised here, and the Arboretum's own account of what came up is worth quoting: the first of its kind to grow in North America in over two million years. The accession number is 524-48. From that lot and its siblings, dawn redwoods went out to gardens across the world, which is how a tree that was a rumour inside living memory became an ordinary sight on ordinary streets.

It stands near the Hunnewell Visitor Center, opposite the Arborway Gate, so it is the first thing worth walking to once you are through. It is also fifteen years older than the dawn redwood in the Public Garden across town, and its senior in the plainest sense: same species, same 1948 seed, one generation up.

One honest note on the record. A separately numbered 1948 accession is described elsewhere as the Arboretum's oldest dawn redwood, out along Conifer Path, and we could not establish whether that is this tree under a second label or a sibling raised from the same seed. Both came off the same shipment.

best_time.label: late October into November, when a conifer this size turns rust orange and drops every needle it has

trees.name: The Wilson Paperbark Maple
trees.age_estimate: roughly 119 years (collected as a wild seedling in 1907)

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, Maple Collection (grid 12-SW), off Meadow Road
location.neighbourhood: Meadow Road, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story:
Almost every paperbark maple in America descends from two seedlings one man dug out of a Chinese wood in the autumn of 1907. The plant collector Ernest Henry Wilson found them in forest north of Yichang, in Hubei, lifted them and shipped them to the Arnold Arboretum. Both survived. This is one of the two, accession 12488, and by the Arboretum's record the pair are the first and the oldest paperbark maples on the continent and the genetic source of most of the ones planted in the country since.

The species has gone the other way at home. Acer griseum is now endangered in the wild in China, its remaining stands small and scattered, which makes a specimen tree in Jamaica Plain a piece of conservation as much as a piece of horticulture.

Come in winter. The bark is what the tree is named for and it is the reason to make the walk: it lifts off the trunk in thin cinnamon and copper curls that stay attached rather than falling, and with the leaves gone and low sun on it the trunk is the whole show.

One note on the record. All of the above traces back to the Arboretum, including a published feature written out of its own history, so this is one institution's account, thorough and public, but not independently corroborated. No coordinates exist for the individual tree. The pin is the maple collection off Meadow Road, about ten minutes up from the Forest Hills gate.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and low winter sun catches the peeling cinnamon bark

trees.name: The Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress

location.address: Bonsai and Penjing Pavilion, Dana Greenhouses, Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, 1050 Centre Street
location.neighbourhood: Dana Greenhouses, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: This tree is 289 years old and it fits on a table. It was started in 1737, when Boston was still a colonial port, and it has spent every one of those years in a pot, watered and pruned by somebody, without a gap. Larz Anderson, a Harvard graduate and American ambassador to Japan, bought it from the Yokohama Nursery Company around 1913 with roughly 39 other bonsai and shipped the lot home to his estate in Brookline, where it stood on his terraces for 24 years. After he and his wife Isabel died, the collection passed to the Arnold Arboretum, which eventually built a pavilion to house it. A cutting taken in 2017 is displayed beside it, the same tree at nine years old and at 289. Two things to know before you go. The 1737 date comes from Anderson's own records rather than from any independent dating, so it is one careful line of evidence repeated by everyone since, not two. And the pavilion rotates around 30 trees through its display every two or three weeks from mid April to late October, so this particular one is not guaranteed to be out on the day you arrive; the pavilion posts what is currently on view. It is ten minutes on foot from Forest Hills, and the Arboretum around it is worth the trip whatever is in the display that week.

trees.name: The Sapporo Katsuras

location.address: Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University, along Meadow Road
location.neighbourhood: Meadow Road, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain

trees.story: These two trees began as seed in a packet posted from Sapporo. William S. Clark, president of Massachusetts Agricultural College and the man who left his Japanese students the parting line "Boys, be ambitious", went to Hokkaido in 1876 to help found what is now Hokkaido University. He collected katsura seed there and sent a share to his friend Charles Sprague Sargent, the Arnold Arboretum's first director. It arrived in 1878, six years after the Arboretum itself existed at all, and the two multi stemmed trees on Meadow Road are what grew from it. They are the oldest katsuras in a collection of 35 and among the oldest documented anywhere in North America. Come in October. Katsura leaves turn apricot and gold, and as they fall and dry they give off a smell most people read as burnt sugar or candy floss; you often catch it before you find the tree. Winter is worth a different look, the silvery grey bark peeling away in narrow rectangular sheets and curved seed follicles hanging on into the cold before the wind takes the seed. Sargent went to Hokkaido himself in 1892 and wrote about katsura as a defining tree of the island's wet lowland woods. One note on sourcing: both accounts here are the Arboretum's own, a plant record and an Arnoldia article rather than two unconnected institutions, though the article's author visited and describes both trees alive and in health.

trees.name: The Longfellow Linden

location.address: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site, 105 Brattle Street, Cambridge, MA
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge (within the day-trip boundary of Boston, roughly 20-25 minutes via Red Line to Harvard Square then a short walk)

trees.story: In the summer of 1844 Henry Wadsworth Longfellow came home to find that workmen had "lopped away the long low branches of my Linden tree, misunderstanding my directions", and he wrote it up in his journal as a small catastrophe. The tree outlived him. It went into the ground around 1800 to 1810, planted by Andrew Craigie, who owned the Brattle Street estate before the poet came to it in 1843, and it stands on the East Lawn of a house that had served as George Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston a generation before the linden existed. Fanny Longfellow wrote in 1843 of wanting "a linden avenue in which my poet intends to pace in his old age". This is the only tree of that avenue still standing. By 1846 he was describing her reading Heine underneath it. The National Park Service puts it at 82 feet, against roughly 60 for the species, with a trunk 84 inches through, and rates its condition fair to poor: the trunk cavity is filled, cables carry the branches, heavy pruning comes round every five years. Since the early 2000s the park has been growing a genetically identical cutting against the day it goes. The grounds are free and open in daylight; only the house tours are ticketed.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the whole East Lawn smells of it

trees.name: The Houghton Beech

location.address: 1000-1008 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA (between Harvard Square and Central Square, on the site of the former Houghton estate, now part of MIT/University Park land)
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge, Mid-Cambridge/University Park (within the day-trip boundary; on the Red Line corridor)

trees.story: This is Cambridge's only living Historic Landmark, and it was made one in 1985 to stop a building. A developer's plans for the site would have taken a third of the copper beech's crown and finished it off, so about thirty neighbours formed a group called the Friends of the Beech Tree and petitioned the city; the Historical Commission designated the tree itself, the legal instrument normally reserved for buildings. The Harvard Crimson, reporting from the October 1985 hearing, called it 203 years old, which puts its planting around 1782 and makes it roughly 240 now. That figure carries more weight than the biography printed around it in the same article, which has Henry O. Houghton serving as mayor decades before he founded the Riverside Press. A 2018 local survey of Cambridge trees offers a looser "planted 150+ years ago", a lower bound rather than a contradiction. Houghton planted three beeches on his family estate here. This is the one left. MIT bought the property in the 1970s and took down the buildings, and the tree stayed, which is how a private estate specimen ended up standing on a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue between Central and Harvard. Most of Boston's notable trees sit inside curated collections. This one you walk past on the way to the bus.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken to purple-black

trees.story:
This is not the tree Newton sat under. It is a living descendant of that one, the apple at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, and it stands in the President's Garden off MIT's Infinite Corridor, where it bears fruit like any other apple tree.

MIT's own facts page records it as a gift from Ed Vetter, class of 1942, and gives no planting date. Nobody appears to have written one down. If you know when it went in, tell us.

What is documented is the morning somebody came to take a piece of it. In 2009 the Tufts cosmologist Alexander Vilenkin asked the MIT physicist Alan Guth about the tree, MIT's president Susan Hockfield gave her permission, and a Tufts grounds manager drove over and cut three branches off it. Those are now a tree in Medford. An apple cultivar only travels by hand, one graft at a time.

The cultivar is worth a sentence. Descendants of the Woolsthorpe tree are 'Flower of Kent' wherever they turn up, a big, coarse cooking apple nobody grows for flavour any more, which is why it is named that way here; MIT's own page does not say so.

MIT's Main Group buildings were reported open to the public on weekdays, 6am to 7pm, in December 2022. That was a few years ago and campus rules move, so treat the hours as a good bet rather than a promise.

trees.story:
Ernest Henry Wilson was already home from his last expedition to Japan when he stopped at a nursery in Yokohama and bought a handful of pine seed almost as an afterthought. That seed, sown at the Arnold Arboretum in 1919, grew into the pine that now greets everyone who climbs Peters Hill Road from the Peters Hill Gate.

A century of wind has done the shaping. The trunk twists rather than rises, and the lower limbs dip low before curling back up, the look Japanese gardeners spend decades training into a tree and this one simply grew into on its own. Two siblings from the same seed lot stand nearby, but the Arboretum's own account singles this one out as the largest and the most sculptural of the three.

Wilson spent years in China and Japan collecting plants for Boston, and the Arboretum still tracks this pine by the same accession number, 11371*J, that a clerk wrote down when it arrived. It turned 100 in 2019 and nobody has found a reason to expect it will stop now.

Every record on this tree traces back to the Arboretum itself, which keeps better books on its own collection than anyone else could. No outside account has turned up yet. If you know one, tell us.

trees.story:
The oldest living cultivated fruit tree in North America grows beside a hospital car park in Danvers, about 25 kilometres north of Boston. It is a pear, planted sometime between 1632 and about 1640 by John Endecott, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and it is the only survivor of his orchard.

It has had a hard four centuries. It came through a storm in 1770. In 1952 a CBS-Hytron plant and its parking lot went up around it until it was nearly hidden. In 1964 vandals took a hacksaw to its branches and trunk and cut it down to about six feet. It grew back. A chain-link fence with barbed wire went up afterwards, and a fence is still what you see it through. The tree once stood about 80 feet tall, by an account from 1875. It is far smaller now.

It still fruits. A December 2024 article reports that it bears pears, a Bon Chrétien sugar pear, and a photograph dated May 2025 shows it standing. If you have seen it since, tell us how it looks.

You cannot walk up to it. The North Shore Medical Center owns it and looks after it with the town, a 2011 marker overlooks it from beside the lot, and a display in the hospital lobby tells its story. From central Boston this is a car trip, or well over an hour by train and bus.

Kew sent the Arnold Arboretum more than 900 plants in its first twenty years, and the Arboretum counts three of them still alive. This beech is one. It arrived in 1885 as a graft, from a line of twisted beeches that goes back to a wild tree in a forest at Remilly, in France. The other two survivors of the Kew exchange are a spiraea and a mock orange.

A parasol beech does not grow up so much as over. Its branches twist and tumble back towards the ground, building a low dome rather than a trunk with a crown on top. The Arboretum's inventory measured the trunk at 93 centimetres across in 2017, about 2.9 metres round, and recorded the tree alive in 2021.

Its age is counted from the day it arrived, so roughly 140 years, and the grafted wood can be a few years older than that. Nobody has written down how tall it is. The Arboretum notes that parasol beeches in the wild can pass 300 years, so by the standard of its own kind this one is not yet old.

About 80 metres to the north-west, just off Beech Path, stands a second parasol beech from Kew, received in 1888 and a little slimmer, its heavy shoots held up by handmade bracing.

The species was first collected only in 1853, by the Scottish plant hunter Robert Fortune, in what is now Zhejiang in eastern China. It is a conifer that behaves like a hardwood. The soft needles sit in spiral rosettes on short spurs, and in late autumn they turn a clear gold and fall, leaving the tree bare all winter.

The two stand about 15 metres apart by Bussey Brook, in a grove of golden larches that also holds an older pair bought directly from Veitch in 1891. In 1980 the Arboretum's journal Arnoldia measured the slimmer of these two at about 12 metres tall and nearly 14 wide, and the Hunnewell parent at about 17. The current inventory records no height. The inventory now gives trunks of 83 and 99 centimetres across, about 3.1 metres round for the larger, and found both in good health in 2023.

Their age is counted from the day the seed arrived, about 130 years. They can be seen from Hemlock Hill Road.

The collection date on this beech is 31 May 1907, in the wild in western Hubei. The director of the Arnold Arboretum gathered the seed of this tree himself. In 1892 Charles Sprague Sargent made his first collecting expedition to Japan, and the Arboretum's own record names him, not a hired collector or a nursery, as the source of this castor aralia. The wild seed was logged in Jamaica Plain on 12 December that year.

It has company from the same trip. Two of its neighbours were also collected in the wild on Sargent's 1892 trip, a konara oak and a Japanese needle juniper, so this corner of the grounds holds three living souvenirs of one journey, still standing close together more than 130 years on.

The castor aralia is an East Asian tree, wild in Japan, and this one has grown into a big one. The inventory measured its trunk at 91.5 centimetres across in July 2021, about 2.9 metres round, and recorded it in good condition. Nobody has written down its height.

Its age is counted from the day the seed arrived, so about 130 years. Because it came as seed rather than as a young plant, that arrival date sits closer to the tree's real age than it would for a tree that arrived as a graft or a nursery plant of unknown years. This oak is a clone of a tree a botanist once described, and its record does not say which tree that was. In February 1883 the Arnold Arboretum received a graft from Dr George Engelmann, the St Louis physician and botanist. A note from the Arboretum's accession card, copied into its records, says that it was taken by Engelmann from the tree described by him.

A graft is a cutting joined onto a rootstock, so the oak growing here is genetically the same individual as Engelmann's original, wherever that stood. The card does not say where, and no source we have identifies it. If you work on Engelmann's papers and recognise the tree, we would very much like to hear.

The clone has done well by its own measure. The inventory gave its trunk as 92.8 centimetres across in 2012, about 2.9 metres round, and lists it among the Arboretum's centenarians, more than 140 years after the graft arrived. Its condition was recorded as fair in 2017, the last check on file, and no height has been measured. That fair rating and the nine-year gap mean nobody has confirmed how it is doing now.

One of this beech's branches grew so long that it put down roots of its own in the flower bed beyond the path. The Friends of the Public Garden, who care for the Garden's trees alongside the city, described it in 2019 as a venerable specimen reaching out over the walkway and over the Bagheera fountain, with that rooted limb cabled back to its many-stemmed trunk to keep the whole thing together.

The Garden holds fourteen beeches, and the Friends say some of them date from its original plantings in the 1870s. The city's tree inventory gives its stems a combined 71 inches across, where the next largest beech is 60.

Age has a cost. In the same 2019 note the Friends reported that the tree was in decline, with significant rot inside, and that they were working to prolong its life, possibly by taking weight off the crown. Only one Japanese pagoda tree in Massachusetts is bigger than this one. The Garden's west side keeps good company. The dawn redwood planted here in 1963 stands about 45 metres away, and a short walk takes in the Garden's biggest ginkgo and its biggest bur oak, all three within about 40 metres of each other. Among the roughly 1,500 trees the city has recorded on Boston Common, in the Public Garden and along the Commonwealth Avenue Mall, there is exactly one rock elm, and it stands near the Public Garden's tool shed. The Friends of the Public Garden call it the lone specimen of its species in all three parks, and the city's inventory agrees.

Rock elm is a North American tree that is rare in cultivation, even in North America. Harvard's Arnold Arboretum titled an article on it "the hard elm that's hard to find", and the title holds up. Seeing one in the middle of a city park is the exception, not the rule, and this one has no relatives nearby to give it away.

This one is a good size, 36 inches across in the city's records, about 2.9 metres round. That is not huge by the standards of the Garden's beeches and oaks, and it does not need to be. Its distinction is the species, not the girth. Walk past it without knowing and it reads as one more elm among the hundreds in these parks.

Nobody has published when it was planted, or why a gardener chose a rock elm for the Public Garden in the first place. If you know either part of that story, tell us. The Bagheera beech and the Garden's lagoon are a short walk away.

It stands a few metres from the Garden's biggest bur oak and about 45 metres from the state's second-largest pagoda tree, so one short loop on the Arlington Street side covers all three. This scarlet oak is older than the cemetery around it. When Mount Auburn opened in 1831, it was already growing here, and the cemetery's plant inventory still files it that way, as received in 1831 and of wild origin. How much older than 1831 it is, nobody knows. The record only says it was here first, which makes it at least 195 years old and possibly a good deal more. trees.story:
Nikko fir grows wild in central Japan, and the biggest one Massachusetts has on record grows between two cemetery paths in Cambridge. The state recorded its champion in Mount Auburn in 2022 at 119.5 inches round and 75.5 feet tall, and the cemetery's own plant inventory has exactly one Nikko fir that fits.

That one stands between Pilgrim Path and Spruce Avenue. The inventory, last checked in October 2025, gives it a trunk 38.5 inches across, about 3.07 metres round, and a height of 77 feet, a shade over 23 metres. The two sets of figures agree within two percent. The state does not name the spot, so the pairing rests on species and size, which is as strong as this kind of match gets without a tag on the trunk.

Nikko fir is not a common sight outside Japan, and a champion of a rare species is a different thing from a champion oak. There may simply be few rivals. It is still a big conifer by any measure, and as an evergreen it looks much the same in every month you could visit.

Mount Auburn opened in 1831, and some 870 of the trees it has mapped since are 30 inches across or more. This is one of them. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.

trees.story:
The champion zelkova of Massachusetts has a crown 93 feet across, wider than the state measured the tree to be tall. That was in 2022, when the register recorded a Japanese zelkova in Mount Auburn Cemetery at 166 inches round, 70.4 feet high and 93 feet from one side of the crown to the other. Japanese zelkova is the register's name for the saw-leaf zelkova.

The register gives no spot within the cemetery. The cemetery's own plant inventory points to this tree by Anemone Path and Mound Avenue, its largest zelkova, at 49 inches across and 84 feet tall. The trunk figures do not quite agree, about seven percent apart, and the inventory measured at two feet off the ground where the state measured at chest height, which accounts for some of it. So this is very likely the champion, and not proven to be.

What you can see for yourself is the spread. A crown nearly 28 metres wide throws a pool of summer shade over a good stretch of the lots beneath it. In autumn the leaves turn yellow to rusty orange, varying from tree to tree.

Nobody has dated it. The inventory gives no planting year, and the cemetery has been planting since 1831. If you know when this one went in, tell us.

trees.story:
The dawn redwood on the Massachusetts big-tree list is not even the largest dawn redwood in Mount Auburn. The state measured one here in February 2022 at 156 inches round and 90 feet tall, and the cemetery's own plant inventory has a tree beside Willow Pond that matches it within one percent on girth and three on height. Over on Rosebay Avenue, though, the inventory has dawn redwoods bigger still, at 55.5 inches across against this one's 49.5, and none of them is on the state list.

So the champion is a champion of the register rather than of the ground, which says more about who got measured than about the trees. The pairing with this pond-side trunk rests on its size, since the state names only the cemetery.

It is a big tree all the same, about 3.95 metres round and 28 metres tall by the inventory's September 2026 figures. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer. It loses its soft needles every autumn, after they turn a reddish brown, which sets it apart from the pines and spruces around it for half the year.

Nobody has published when it was planted, which matters for a species science only described from living trees in the 1940s. An early date would make it one of the first in the country. If you know the story, tell us. About 25 metres away, by Sedum Path, stands the cemetery's tall Himalayan pine.

trees.story:
This pine stands 101 feet tall, close to 31 metres, and its species comes from the Himalaya. The cemetery's own plant inventory measured it in September 2026, with a trunk 32.75 inches across, about 2.61 metres round, which is slender for that height. It is built upward rather than outward.

Massachusetts lists its champion Himalayan pine in Mount Auburn, measured in 2022 at 96 inches round and 91.1 feet tall. The state gives no position inside the cemetery, and this is the only Himalayan pine of any size in the inventory, so it is almost certainly the same tree. The figures sit about seven percent apart, and the state's height is ten feet lower, so read the champion title as very likely rather than certain.

It keeps its needles all year, so the tree you see in February is the tree you see in July. Its neighbour 25 metres away by Willow Pond is a dawn redwood, a conifer that does the opposite and stands bare from November.

Nobody has published a planting date for it, and the inventory gives none. If you know when it went in, tell us.

trees.story:
The next biggest Norway spruce in Mount Auburn's plant inventory is 36.5 inches across. This one is 56. That gap is wide enough that the cemetery's record and the state's both point at it, even though neither says so outright.

Massachusetts lists a champion Norway spruce in the cemetery, measured in February 2022 at 194 inches round and 69.5 feet tall, with no position given. The inventory's figure for this tree on Indian Ridge Path is 177 inches round, taken just six inches above the ground, across the flare of the roots, and a height of 65 feet. A measurement that low flatters any trunk, so the comparison with the other spruces is not quite like for like. Even so, nothing else in the cemetery comes close, and the champion is very probably this tree.

Norway spruce is a European tree, a long way from home in a Cambridge cemetery. It is evergreen, so it looks the same in every season, and with the cedar of Lebanon about 30 metres away it makes a short winter walk of two conifers.

The inventory gives no planting year and nobody has published one. The cemetery has been planting since 1831, which bounds the question without answering it. If you know when this spruce went in, tell us.

trees.story:
Mount Auburn's plant inventory gives this red oak a trunk 68 inches across, a figure so large it may take in a second stem. Even allowing for that, it is the biggest red oak the cemetery has on record, about 31 metres tall, and it was here before the cemetery was.

The inventory files it as received in 1831 and of wild origin, which is its way of saying the tree was already growing when Mount Auburn opened that year. That makes it at least 195 years old, with no record of how much older. It stands in the section where Lime and Fountain avenues meet, and everything around it, every lot and every monument, came later.

What it does not have is a state title. Massachusetts lists several Mount Auburn trees as champions, but no red oak among the cemetery's rows, so the only measurements here are the cemetery's own, last checked in August 2026 and measured that September. The 5.7-foot diameter is worth taking with some caution for the reason above. The height, 103 feet, needs no such hedge.

It is one of two big oaks the inventory records as older than the cemetery. The other is the scarlet oak by Moss Path, taller and slimmer. This one is the heavyweight. About 40 metres away in the same section stands the cemetery's biggest katsura.

trees.story:
Massachusetts gives directions to its second-largest London plane in five words, one of them misspelled. The register line reads "Accross from 40 York St", in Wellington-Harrington, and nobody has published a better address.

The tree behind that line is 480 centimetres round, 79 feet tall and 79.5 feet across the crown, so it is very nearly as wide as it is high, about 24 metres both ways. The state measured it in August 2025. Only one London plane in the state is bigger.

It is a street tree, not a park tree. There is no fence, no lawn and no visitor path, just a residential block in east Cambridge and a crown that spreads over it.

Our pin sits on the building at number 40, because that is what can be placed. The tree is across the road from it, perhaps 20 metres off. Look for the crown, which at that width should be hard to miss on a residential street.

Nobody has dated it, and the register gives no planting year. If you live on York Street and know its history, tell us.
